questions.question: Which ancient people built the pyramids at Giza?
questions.explanation: The Giza pyramids were tombs for pharaohs. They were built about 4,500 years ago from huge blocks of stone.

questions.question: What was the title of an ancient Egyptian king?
questions.explanation: Pharaoh first meant 'great house', the king's palace. Later it became the name for the king himself.

questions.question: Where in Greece were the ancient Olympic Games held?
questions.explanation: The ancient Games took place every four years at Olympia. The modern Olympic Games began in Athens in 1896.

questions.question: Which reed plant did ancient Egyptians use to make sheets to write on?
questions.explanation: Papyrus grew along the Nile. Strips of it were pressed together and dried. The English word 'paper' comes from it.

questions.question: Which ancient people built the Colosseum in their capital city?
questions.explanation: The Colosseum in Rome opened in AD 80. Crowds went there to watch fights and shows.

questions.question: Why was the Great Wall of China built?
questions.explanation: Rulers of China joined older walls together over many centuries. The wall had towers where guards could watch for enemies.

questions.question: Which animal did ancient Egyptians value for keeping mice away from their grain?
questions.explanation: Egyptians loved cats so much that they made statues of them. Some cats were even made into mummies.

questions.question: What are bodies called that ancient Egyptians dried and wrapped in cloth?
questions.explanation: Egyptians believed people needed their body in the next life. So they took great care to preserve it.

questions.question: Which Greek city is famous for the first democracy?
questions.explanation: In Athens, citizens voted on laws themselves. Not everyone could vote: women, slaves and foreigners were left out.

questions.question: Which animals did the general Hannibal take across the Alps to attack Rome?
questions.explanation: Hannibal came from Carthage in North Africa. He crossed the snowy Alps in about 218 BC with an army and elephants.

questions.question: What number does the Roman numeral X stand for?
questions.explanation: Romans used letters for numbers: I is 1, V is 5, X is 10, L is 50 and C is 100. We still see them on some clocks.

questions.question: Which famous queen ruled Egypt about 2,000 years ago and met Julius Caesar?
questions.explanation: Cleopatra spoke many languages. She was the last queen of ancient Egypt before it became part of the Roman Empire.

questions.question: What is the name of the thousands of life-size soldier statues buried with China's first emperor?
questions.explanation: Farmers found the statues in 1974. Each soldier has a different face. Terracotta is a kind of baked clay.

questions.question: What was the Parthenon in Athens?
questions.explanation: The Parthenon was built on a hill called the Acropolis about 2,500 years ago. It was a temple for the goddess Athena.

questions.question: What did the Romans build to carry water into their cities?
questions.explanation: Roman aqueducts let water flow slowly downhill, often over tall stone arches. Some of them are still standing.

questions.question: What was the picture writing of ancient Egypt called?
questions.explanation: Hieroglyphs used little pictures of birds, eyes, snakes and more. Few people could read them, and scribes learned for years.

questions.question: Chichen Itza has a famous stepped pyramid. Which ancient people built it?
questions.explanation: The Maya lived in Mexico and Central America. They built cities, studied the stars and had their own writing.

questions.question: Which young king of Macedonia built a huge empire and is called 'the Great'?
questions.explanation: Alexander became king at 20. In about 13 years he led his army from Greece all the way to India.

questions.question: Which Roman leader was killed by a group of senators in 44 BC?
questions.explanation: Some senators feared Caesar was getting too much power. His death led to more years of civil war in Rome.

questions.question: What did Romans do at the public baths?
questions.explanation: Roman baths had hot and cold pools. They were also places to talk, play games and do business.

questions.question: The Great Sphinx of Giza has the body of which animal?
questions.explanation: The Sphinx was carved from the rock beside the pyramids. It has a lion's body and the head of a human.

questions.question: Bronze is made by mixing copper with which other metal?
questions.explanation: Bronze is harder than copper, so it made better tools and weapons. It gave its name to the Bronze Age.

questions.question: The Asterix comics are about a village of which ancient people fighting the Romans?
questions.explanation: The Gauls were Celtic people who lived in what is now France. The real Julius Caesar conquered Gaul.

questions.question: What was the main language of the ancient Romans?
questions.explanation: Italian, French, Spanish and Portuguese all grew out of Latin. Many English words come from it too.

questions.question: Which ancient Greek city was famous for its tough soldiers?
questions.explanation: Spartan boys started training for war when they were about seven years old. In English, 'spartan' means plain and without comforts.

questions.question: Which Greek inventor is said to have shouted 'Eureka!' in his bath?
questions.explanation: The story says he saw that his body pushed out water as he sat in the bath. This gave him a way to measure the size of objects.

questions.question: Which creature's cocoons did people in ancient China use to make fine, shiny cloth?
questions.explanation: The cloth is silk. China kept the secret of making it for centuries and sold silk along the Silk Road.

questions.question: Mesopotamia lay between the Tigris and which other river?
questions.explanation: Mesopotamia means 'the land between the rivers'. Some of the first cities in the world grew there.

questions.question: Which hard building material did the Romans make from lime, volcanic ash and stones?
questions.explanation: Roman concrete helped them build huge domes and arches. The dome of the Pantheon in Rome is almost 2,000 years old.

questions.question: Which young pharaoh's tomb, full of gold and treasure, was found in 1922?
questions.explanation: Tutankhamun became king as a child and died young. His tomb was found almost untouched, with his famous gold mask inside.

questions.question: What was the long robe wrapped around the body that Roman men wore?
questions.explanation: Only Roman citizens could wear a toga. Most togas were plain white, and important officials wore one with a purple edge.

questions.question: Paper was first made in which ancient country about 2,000 years ago?
questions.explanation: Early Chinese paper was made from rags and bark. The skill spread west slowly along the Silk Road.

questions.question: Which Roman town was buried by ash when Mount Vesuvius erupted?
questions.explanation: The ash kept the town almost as it was in AD 79. We can see houses, shops and even paintings on the walls.

questions.question: What did people in ancient Mesopotamia press signs into when they wrote?
questions.explanation: Their writing was made with a pointed reed pressed into soft clay. It is called cuneiform, meaning wedge-shaped.

questions.question: What did winners of the ancient Olympic Games get as a prize?
questions.explanation: Winners also became famous heroes in their home cities. Olive trees were special to the Greeks.

questions.question: Which British queen led a revolt against the Romans in about AD 60?
questions.explanation: Boudicca was queen of the Iceni tribe in eastern Britain. Her army burned three Roman towns, among them early London.

questions.question: The Library of Alexandria in Egypt was famous for holding thousands of what?
questions.explanation: Books were rolls of papyrus. Scholars from many lands came to read and copy them.

questions.question: Which ancient tool used a shadow to tell the time?
questions.explanation: A shadow moved across marks as the Sun crossed the sky. A sundial does not work at night or on a cloudy day.

questions.question: The Nile flooded every year. Why was this good for Egyptian farmers?
questions.correct: It left rich mud on the land
wrong: It brought salt to the soil
questions.explanation: The mud made the soil very fertile. The Egyptians called their farmland 'the black land' and the desert 'the red land'.

questions.question: Confucius was a wise teacher from which ancient land?
questions.explanation: Confucius lived about 2,500 years ago. His ideas about respect and good behaviour spread across East Asia.

questions.question: Which woman ruled Egypt as pharaoh about 3,500 years ago and was shown wearing a false beard?
questions.explanation: Hatshepsut ruled for about 20 years. Pharaohs were shown with a beard, so she had herself shown with one too.

questions.question: What did the Rosetta Stone help scholars to read?
questions.explanation: It has the same text in three scripts, including Greek. In 1822 Jean-François Champollion used it to understand hieroglyphs.

questions.question: Cuneiform writing was first used by which ancient people?
questions.explanation: The Sumerians lived in southern Mesopotamia more than 5,000 years ago. They first wrote to keep records of trade and grain.

questions.question: Which king of Babylon is famous for a list of laws carved on a stone pillar, about 1750 BC?
questions.explanation: The laws on it cover trade, family life and crime. Punishments often depended on a person's rank in society.

questions.question: Which river did Julius Caesar cross in 49 BC, starting a civil war in Rome?
questions.explanation: Crossing it with an army broke Roman law. The phrase 'crossing the Rubicon' means making a choice you cannot take back.

questions.question: Who became the first Roman emperor, in 27 BC?
questions.explanation: Augustus was Julius Caesar's great-nephew and adopted son. The month of August is named after him.

questions.question: In 490 BC the Greeks beat which empire at the Battle of Marathon?
questions.explanation: The marathon race is named after this battle. A legend says a runner took the news to Athens.

questions.question: Which Spartan king led the small Greek force at Thermopylae in 480 BC?
questions.explanation: Leonidas and his men held a narrow mountain pass against the huge Persian army for days.

questions.question: How often were the ancient Olympic Games held?
questions.explanation: A truce let athletes and visitors travel safely to Olympia, even when Greek cities were at war.

questions.question: Which Roman emperor gave his name to a wall across northern Britain?
questions.explanation: Work on the wall began in about AD 122. It marked the edge of the Roman Empire and was guarded by soldiers.

questions.question: Which year is usually given for the end of the Western Roman Empire?
questions.explanation: In 476 the last Western emperor, a boy named Romulus Augustulus, was removed from power. The Eastern Empire lasted for about 1,000 years more.

questions.question: Which Roman emperor made the old Greek town of Byzantium his new capital in AD 330?
questions.explanation: He renamed it Constantinople, 'the city of Constantine'. Much later, the city became known as Istanbul.

questions.question: In the Punic Wars, Rome fought which rival city in North Africa?
questions.explanation: Carthage was a rich trading city founded by Phoenicians. After the third war, in 146 BC, Rome destroyed it.

questions.question: For which pharaoh was the Great Pyramid of Giza built?
questions.explanation: It was built about 2560 BC and was the tallest building in the world for more than 3,800 years.

questions.question: Which Greek thinker taught the young Alexander the Great?
questions.explanation: Aristotle wrote about science, politics and poetry. He was himself a student of Plato.

questions.question: Which ancient Greek doctor is called the 'father of medicine'?
questions.explanation: Hippocrates taught that illness has natural causes. A famous promise made by doctors, the Hippocratic oath, is named after him.

questions.question: Which Greek writer is called the 'father of history'?
questions.explanation: Herodotus travelled widely and wrote about the Persian Wars. He asked people questions to find out what really happened.

questions.question: What was the Roman system of heating floors and walls with hot air called?
questions.explanation: A fire sent hot air under raised floors and through the walls. Rich homes and baths in Roman Britain had it too.

questions.question: Which ancient Chinese thinker is traditionally said to have written The Art of War?
questions.explanation: The book is about planning, strategy and knowing your enemy. Generals have studied it for centuries.

questions.question: Harappa and Mohenjo-daro were cities of an ancient civilisation named after which river?
questions.explanation: Mohenjo-daro stood beside the Indus. These cities had straight streets, brick houses and drains, and traded as far as Mesopotamia.

questions.question: Who founded the Persian Empire around 550 BC?
questions.explanation: Cyrus the Great's empire stretched from the Aegean Sea to Central Asia. He is remembered for treating the peoples he ruled with respect.

questions.question: Which ancient civilisation on the island of Crete built the palace of Knossos?
questions.explanation: The Minoans were at their height about 3,500 to 4,000 years ago. They were great sailors and traders, and their palaces had paintings of dolphins.

questions.question: What were the learned priests and teachers of the ancient Celts called?
questions.explanation: Druids learned long poems by heart rather than writing them. We know about them mostly from Greek and Roman writers.

questions.question: Which food plant was the main crop of the ancient Maya?
questions.explanation: The Maya ate maize in many ways, such as tamales and porridge. They also grew cacao and made a chocolate drink from its beans.

questions.question: What number does the Roman numeral D stand for?
questions.explanation: Romans wrote 1,000 as M. They had no sign for zero, which made sums with Roman numerals hard.

questions.question: Which organ did Egyptian embalmers leave in the body, believing it held thought and feeling?
questions.explanation: The brain was thrown away. The liver, lungs, stomach and intestines were dried and kept in special jars.

questions.question: The Pharos, one of the Seven Wonders, was a lighthouse in which city?
questions.explanation: The Pharos was built on an island by Alexandria's harbour. It stood for more than 1,500 years until earthquakes brought it down.

questions.question: In the Roman Republic, what were the two top leaders, elected each year, called?
questions.explanation: Two consuls shared power, so that no single man would rule alone. Under the emperors there were still consuls, but they had little real power.

questions.question: Which gladiator led a big slave revolt against Rome in 73 BC?
questions.explanation: Spartacus gathered tens of thousands of followers. The Romans needed several armies to defeat them.

questions.question: Which Roman emperor ruled during the Great Fire of Rome in AD 64?
questions.explanation: A famous story says he played music while Rome burned. Most historians doubt it, and he may not even have been in the city.

questions.question: Doric, Ionic and Corinthian are styles of what in ancient Greek buildings?
questions.explanation: You can tell them apart by the top of the column. Doric is plain, Ionic has scrolls and Corinthian has carved leaves.

questions.question: Roman chariot races were held at which huge track in Rome?
questions.explanation: The track could hold many thousands of spectators. Teams were known by their colours.

questions.question: What was the Colossus of Rhodes, one of the Seven Wonders?
questions.explanation: It stood near the harbour of the Greek island of Rhodes. An earthquake knocked it down less than 60 years after it was finished.

questions.question: What were the huge stepped temple towers of ancient Mesopotamia called?
questions.explanation: A ziggurat was built of mud bricks in several layers. A shrine stood at the top.

questions.question: What was the agora in an ancient Greek city?
questions.explanation: People bought food there and talked about politics. The Agora of Athens lay below the Acropolis.

questions.question: Which ancient seafaring people from the Lebanon coast were famous for purple dye?
questions.explanation: The dye came from sea snails and was so costly that purple became the colour of kings and emperors.

questions.question: Which two Greek city-states fought the long Peloponnesian War?
questions.explanation: The war lasted about 27 years, from 431 BC. Sparta won, but all of Greece grew weaker.

questions.question: On how many hills is the city of Rome said to be built?
questions.explanation: Rome grew from small villages on hills beside the River Tiber. The Palatine and the Capitoline are two of the seven.

questions.question: What did the Romans call Britain?
questions.explanation: Britannia was a Roman province for almost 400 years. Caledonia was their name for the land in the far north.

questions.question: What was London called when it was a Roman town?
questions.explanation: Londinium was founded in about AD 47, soon after the Romans arrived. It grew beside the River Thames, where they built a bridge.

questions.question: Which Greek scholar in Alexandria measured the size of the Earth around 240 BC?
questions.explanation: He compared the Sun's shadow in two Egyptian cities. His answer was close to the real size.

questions.question: Which Indian emperor of the 200s BC turned to peace after a bloody war and spread Buddhism?
questions.explanation: Ashoka had his laws carved on pillars and rocks across his empire. The lion top of one of his pillars became India's national emblem.

questions.question: In which battle in 216 BC did Hannibal beat a much larger Roman army?
questions.explanation: Hannibal surrounded the Romans from both sides. For centuries, generals have studied the battle as a model of tactics.

questions.question: Which Roman general beat Hannibal at the Battle of Zama in 202 BC?
questions.explanation: Scipio took the war to Carthage's homeland in North Africa. The title 'Africanus' was given to him after his victory.

questions.question: At the Battle of Actium in 31 BC, Octavian defeated which pair?
questions.explanation: After the sea battle, Antony and Cleopatra fled to Egypt. Octavian soon took Egypt and became Augustus.

questions.question: Which Persian king invaded Greece in 480 BC after building a bridge of boats across the Hellespont?
questions.explanation: The Hellespont, also called the Dardanelles, is a narrow strait in Turkey. Xerxes's huge army crossed from Asia into Europe on the bridge.

questions.question: Which Athenian's plan led to the Greek sea victory over the Persians at Salamis in 480 BC?
questions.explanation: He tempted the Persian ships into a narrow channel, where their larger numbers were of little help.

questions.question: Cleopatra belonged to which Greek-speaking royal family of Egypt?
questions.explanation: The family began with Ptolemy, one of Alexander the Great's generals. Cleopatra is said to have been the first of them to learn Egyptian.

questions.question: Which seafaring people spread the alphabet that the Greeks later adapted?
questions.explanation: Their alphabet had only letters for consonants. The Greeks added letters for vowels, and our alphabet grew from theirs.

questions.question: Linear B tablets, found at Knossos and Pylos, were shown to record an early form of which language?
questions.explanation: Michael Ventris worked this out in 1952. The tablets are mostly lists of goods, not stories.

questions.question: Which ancient African kingdom south of Egypt once ruled Egypt and built its own pyramids?
questions.explanation: Kush was in what is now Sudan. Its kings ruled Egypt as pharaohs for nearly 100 years, from around 750 BC.

questions.question: Which Roman emperor split rule between four co-rulers around AD 293?
questions.explanation: The empire was hard to rule and defend from one place. The system was called the tetrarchy, meaning 'rule of four'.

questions.question: Under which emperor did the Roman Empire reach its largest size, in AD 117?
questions.explanation: Trajan conquered Dacia and parts of the Middle East. His successor Hadrian gave up some of the new land.

questions.question: Which pharaoh tried to make Egyptians worship only the sun disc Aten?
questions.explanation: Akhenaten built a new capital, Amarna. After he died, the old ways returned, and his city was left empty.

questions.question: Ramses II fought the Hittites at which battle, around 1274 BC?
questions.explanation: Both sides said they had won. Later they made one of the oldest peace treaties we know of.

questions.question: Which Roman writer described the AD 79 eruption of Vesuvius in letters?
questions.explanation: He watched from across the bay, aged 17. His uncle, Pliny the Elder, died while trying to rescue people.

questions.question: What is the round opening at the top of the Pantheon's dome in Rome called?
questions.explanation: Oculus means 'eye'. Rain falls through it, and the floor has holes to let the water drain away.

questions.question: What was the short stabbing sword of a Roman legionary called?
questions.explanation: The gladius was good for close fighting in tight ranks. The pilum was a throwing spear, and the scutum was the big shield.

questions.question: Which Gaulish chief surrendered to Julius Caesar after the siege of Alesia in 52 BC?
questions.explanation: He had united many Gaulish tribes against Rome. After the defeat, Gaul became a Roman land for hundreds of years.

questions.question: In AD 9, which Germanic leader destroyed three Roman legions in the Teutoburg Forest?
questions.explanation: The defeat shocked Rome. Afterwards the Rhine stayed the empire's border for centuries.

questions.question: Which Gothic king and his army sacked Rome in AD 410?
questions.explanation: It was the first time in about 800 years that an enemy had taken the city of Rome.

questions.question: Which ancient empire built the Royal Road, with relay riders, from Sardis to Susa?
questions.explanation: Fresh riders and horses waited at stations along the road, so messages travelled far faster than people on foot.

questions.question: The Behistun Inscription helped scholars to read which kind of writing?
questions.explanation: Darius I had the same text carved in three languages on a cliff in Persia. Henry Rawlinson copied it in the 1830s and 1840s.

questions.question: Which king of Babylon rebuilt the city and its famous Ishtar Gate?
questions.explanation: His Babylon was one of the biggest cities in the world. The gate was covered with blue glazed bricks.

questions.question: King Ashurbanipal of Assyria is famous for collecting what in his capital, Nineveh?
questions.explanation: Thousands of his tablets survived, because fire only baked the clay harder. They hold poems, letters and science.

questions.question: Who founded the Maurya Empire in India around 321 BC?
questions.explanation: Chandragupta's empire covered most of northern India. His grandson Ashoka later ruled it.

questions.question: Which Chinese dynasty opened the Silk Road trade routes to the West?
questions.explanation: The Han emperor Wu sent the envoy Zhang Qian to Central Asia. The trip led to trade with Persia and beyond.

questions.question: Which natural substance did Egyptians use to dry out bodies when making mummies?
questions.explanation: Natron is a salt that came from dry lake beds. It took about 40 days to dry a body before it was wrapped.

questions.question: Which Athenian leader's reforms in 508 BC are said to have started democracy there?
questions.explanation: Cleisthenes divided the citizens into new groups and set up a council. He is often called the father of Athenian democracy.

questions.question: In ancient Sparta, who were the helots?
questions.explanation: Helots grew the food so that Spartan men could spend their lives training for war. They outnumbered the Spartans.

questions.question: Which city led the Delian League, formed in 478 BC after the Persian Wars?
questions.explanation: Members paid money or ships to protect against Persia. Athens later used the league's money to build the Parthenon.

questions.question: What was the name of Alexander the Great's famous horse?
questions.explanation: Alexander tamed Bucephalus as a boy, when no one else could ride him. He later named a city after the horse.

questions.question: In which city did Alexander the Great die in 323 BC?
questions.explanation: He was only 32. His generals split his empire between them, and wars over it lasted for decades.

questions.question: Alexander the Great beat which Persian king at the Battle of Gaugamela in 331 BC?
questions.explanation: Darius fled, and was later killed by his own men. Alexander then took Babylon and the Persian capitals.

questions.question: Which Roman historian wrote 'Germania', describing the tribes beyond the Rhine?
questions.explanation: Tacitus wrote it in about AD 98, probably using reports from traders and soldiers. It is a main source on early Germanic peoples.

questions.question: What were the Twelve Tables of about 450 BC?
questions.explanation: They were carved on bronze or wood and put up in the Forum. Roman children learned them by heart.

questions.question: Which Roman senator ended speeches by urging that Carthage must be destroyed?
questions.explanation: Carthage was destroyed in 146 BC, three years after Cato died.

questions.question: Which people, led by Brennus, took Rome in about 390 BC?
questions.explanation: The Romans said that geese on the Capitoline Hill raised the alarm. Rome built strong walls afterwards.

questions.question: The great Maya city of Tikal lies in the jungle of which country?
questions.explanation: Tikal had tall stepped pyramids, and many thousands of people lived there. It was at its peak about 1,300 years ago.

questions.question: Which ancient city in Mexico, with the Pyramid of the Sun, was already in ruins when the Aztecs found it?
questions.explanation: The name comes from the Aztecs and is often translated as 'place where the gods were born'. We do not know what its builders called it.
